Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe safety of those who have God for their refuge.1–8Their favour with Him.9–16
God is the believer's refuge (verses 1–8)

Those who choose God as their protector through faith will find in him everything they need or can rightly desire.

People who have experienced that comfort want others to find refuge in him too.

God's grace preserves spiritual life from Satan's temptations, pictured as the traps of a birdcatcher, and from the contagion of sin, pictured as a deadly disease.

Great security is promised to believers even when they are surrounded by danger.

Wisdom prevents groundless fear; faith keeps us from being overwhelmed by justified fear.

Whatever happens, our heavenly Father's will is fulfilled. We need not be ruled by terror.

God's people will see both his promises fulfilled and his warnings carried out.

Therefore sinners should approach his mercy seat through the Redeemer's name and encourage others to trust him.

God's care in trouble and at life's end (verses 9–16)

No event can ultimately harm a believer.

Trouble and suffering may still come.

They can be painful rather than pleasant for the present, but God will make them work for the believer's good.

Those who truly know God will love him and continually call upon him in prayer.

His promise is to deliver the believer in his appointed time and, meanwhile, to be with that believer in trouble.

The Lord will govern their earthly concerns and preserve their lives as long as remaining here is truly good for them.

They look to Jesus for encouragement.

The believer will live long enough to complete the work assigned by God and become ready for heaven.

Why would anyone want an additional day after God had no further work to do in them or through them?

Someone may die young yet have a satisfying life.

A wicked person, by contrast, may live for many years without ever being satisfied.

At last the believer's struggle ends.

Then sin, suffering and temptation are gone forever.

Chapter 91
Chapter Outline
The safety of those who have God for their refuge. | (1-8) |
Their favour with Him. | (9-16) |
Verses 1-8
He that by faith chooses God for his protector, shall find all in him that he needs or can desire. And those who have found the comfort of making the Lord their refuge, cannot but desire that others may do so. The spiritual life is protected by Divine grace from the temptations of Satan, which are as the snares of the fowler, and from the contagion of sin, which is a noisome pestilence. Great security is promised to believers in the midst of danger. Wisdom shall keep them from being afraid without cause, and faith shall keep them from being unduly afraid. Whatever is done, our heavenly Father's will is done; and we have no reason to fear. God's people shall see, not only God's promises fulfilled, but his threatenings. Then let sinners come unto the Lord upon his mercy-seat, through the Redeemer's name; and encourage others to trust in him also.
[Ps.91.9-Ps.91.16]
Verses 9-16
Whatever happens, nothing shall hurt the believer; though trouble and affliction befal, it shall come, not for his hurt, but for good, though for the present it be not joyous but grievous. Those who rightly know God, will set their love upon him. They by prayer constantly call upon him. His promise is, that he will in due time deliver the believer out of trouble, and in the mean time be with him in trouble. The Lord will manage all his worldly concerns, and preserve his life on earth, so long as it shall be good for him. For encouragement in this he looks unto Jesus. He shall live long enough; till he has done the work he was sent into this world for, and is ready for heaven. Who would wish to live a day longer than God has some work to do, either by him or upon him? A man may die young, yet be satisfied with living. But a wicked man is not satisfied even with long life. At length the believer's conflict ends; he has done for ever with trouble, sin, and temptation.

Thanksgiving on the Sabbath and every day (verses 1–6)

It is a privilege to praise the Lord and hope that he will accept our worship morning and evening.

This is not only for the Sabbath, but for every day; not only in public gatherings, but also alone and with our families.

Each morning, thank him for the mercies of the night.

Each evening, thank him for the mercies of the day.

When going out or coming home, bless his name.

His work of Providence toward us, his work of grace within us, and above all his great work of redemption give us reason for joy.

Many people neither know nor care about his purposes.

Those who have learned to appreciate them through grace have even greater reason for gratitude.

If the ancient believers rejoiced in distant glimpses of the promised Deliverer, how much more should we love and praise him!

Brief prosperity and lasting fruitfulness (verses 7–15)

God sometimes allows wicked people to prosper as a judgment against them.

Their flourishing lasts only briefly.

Let us therefore seek the salvation and grace of the gospel, so that the Holy Spirit continually anoints us and we may see and share in the Redeemer's glory.

Christ's grace, communicated through his word and Spirit, supplies everything that keeps believers spiritually alive and fruitful.

Ordinary trees cease bearing fruit as they grow old.

But in God's trees, spiritual strength need not fade as bodily strength diminishes.

The final days of faithful people may be their best, and their last work their finest.

Perseverance is reliable evidence of sincerity.

May every Sabbath, as we contemplate God's faithfulness, find us resting more firmly upon the Lord our righteousness.
classic_reading:
[Ps.92.1-Ps.92.6]
Chapter 92
Chapter Outline
Praise is the business of the sabbath. | (1-6) |
The wicked shall perish, but God's people shall be exalted. | (7-15) |
Verses 1-6
It is a privilege that we are admitted to praise the Lord, and hope to be accepted in the morning, and every night; not only on sabbath days, but every day; not only in public, but in private, and in our families. Let us give thanks every morning for the mercies of the night, and every night for the mercies of the day; going out, and coming in, let us bless God. As He makes us glad, through the works of his providence for us, and of his grace in us, and both through the great work of redemption, let us hence be encouraged. As there are many who know not the designs of Providence, nor care to know them, those who through grace do so, have the more reason to be thankful. And if distant views of the great Deliverer so animated believers of old, how should we abound in love and praise!
[Ps.92.7-Ps.92.15]
Verses 7-15
God sometimes grants prosperity to wicked men in displeasure; yet they flourish but for a moment. Let us seek for ourselves the salvation and grace of the gospel, that being daily anointed by the Holy Spirit, we may behold and share the Redeemer's glory. It is from his grace, by his word and Spirit, that believers receive all the virtue that keeps them alive, and makes them fruitful. Other trees, when old, leave off bearing, but in God's trees the strength of grace does not fail with the strength of nature. The last days of the saints are sometimes their best days, and their last work their best work: perseverance is sure evidence of sincerity. And may every sabbath, while it shows forth the Divine faithfulness, find our souls resting more and more upon the Lord our righteousness.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The majesty, power, and holiness of Christ's kingdom.

The majesty and holiness of Christ's kingdom

God could have revealed only his justice, holiness and fearful power in dealing with fallen humanity.

Instead, he has chosen to reveal the riches of his mercy and the power of his renewing grace.

In this great work the Father has given all authority to his Son, the Lord from heaven, who has made atonement for our sins.

Christ is able not only to pardon, but also to deliver and protect everyone who trusts in him.

He has given his word, and all God's people may rely upon it.

Everything foretold about the Messiah's kingdom will be fulfilled at the appointed time.

His people ought to live in strict holiness.

The church is God's own house, set apart from sin and devoted to his service.

Where purity is found, peace will follow.

Let each person examine carefully whether this kingdom has been established within the heart.
classic_reading:

Chapter 93
The majesty, power, and holiness of Christ's kingdom.
--The Lord might have displayed only his justice, holiness, and awful power, in his dealings with fallen men; but he has been pleased to display the riches of his mercy, and the power of his renewing grace. In this great work, the Father has given all power to his Son, the Lord from heaven, who has made atonement for our sins. He not only can pardon, but deliver and protect all who trust in him. His word is past, and all the saints may rely upon it. Whatever was foretold concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, must be fulfilled in due time. All his people ought to be very strictly pure. God's church is his house; it is a holy house, cleansed from sin, and employed in his service. Where there is purity, there shall be peace. Let all carefully look if this kingdom is set up in their hearts.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe danger and folly of persecutors.1–11Comfort and peace to the persecuted.12–23
Entrusting injustice to the righteous Judge (verses 1–11)

We may appeal to God with confidence because he is the almighty Judge before whom everyone must answer.

Those treated unjustly can be encouraged to endure the wrong without seeking private retaliation, entrusting their cause to the One who judges righteously.

Henry understands these prayers as prophetic warnings to violent people.

A day of reckoning will come for all the arrogant and cruel words ungodly people have spoken against God, his truth, his ways and his servants.

It is astonishing how many rational people live, think, speak, hear and act freely while behaving as though the Lord will never call them to account for misusing his gifts.

Every form of knowledge comes from him, so he certainly knows every human thought.

The inclinations of fallen hearts are continually evil.

Even thoughts that are good in themselves may be wandering and unsettled; this too can be called vanity.

We must therefore watch our thoughts carefully.

God notices them all.

Our thoughts are words before him.

The comfort of divine correction and care (verses 12–23)

Blessed is the person whom God disciplines and teaches his truth through Scripture and the Holy Spirit.

Such a person can recognize mercy even within suffering.

Rest remains for God's people after their days of trouble, which will not continue forever.

The same Lord who sends affliction will also send relief.

When the psalmist's earthly friends failed him, he found help only in God.

We depend not only upon God's power, but also upon his compassion, to keep us spiritually secure.

If he preserves us from falling into sin or abandoning duty, all glory belongs to him.

We should share that encouragement with others.

The psalmist had many anxious thoughts about his situation, what he should do and how things might end.

Indulging such anxious speculation and fear adds to our cares and weakens trust, making circumstances appear darker and more confused.

Even faithful believers can be troubled by distressing thoughts about God.

They should return to the great and precious promises of the gospel.

Worldly comforts offer little relief to a soul overwhelmed by melancholy.

But God's consolation gives a peace the world cannot provide or remove.

God is his people's refuge, where they may safely shelter.

He will also judge wickedness.

No one can be made more miserable than their own wrongdoing will make them when the Lord finally calls it to account.
classic_reading:
[Ps.94.1-Ps.94.11]
Chapter 94
Chapter Outline
The danger and folly of persecutors. | (1-11) |
Comfort and peace to the persecuted. | (12-23) |
Verses 1-11
We may with boldness appeal to God; for he is the almighty Judge by whom every man is judged. Let this encourage those who suffer wrong, to bear it with silence, committing themselves to Him who judges righteously. These prayers are prophecies, which speak terror to the sons of violence. There will come a day of reckoning for all the hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against God, his truths, and ways, and people. It would hardly be believed, if we did not witness it, that millions of rational creatures should live, move, speak, hear, understand, and do what they purpose, yet act as if they believed that God would not punish the abuse of his gifts. As all knowledge is from God, no doubt he knows all the thoughts of the children of men, and knows that the imaginations of the thoughts of men's hearts are only evil, and that continually. Even in good thoughts there is a want of being fixed, which may be called vanity. It concerns us to keep a strict watch over our thoughts, because God takes particular notice of them. Thoughts are words to God.
[Ps.94.12-Ps.94.23]
Verses 12-23
That man is blessed, who, under the chastening of the Lord, is taught his will and his truths, from his holy word, and by the Holy Spirit. He should see mercy through his sufferings. There is a rest remaining for the people of God after the days of their adversity, which shall not last always. He that sends the trouble, will send the rest. The psalmist found succour and relief only in the Lord, when all earthly friends failed. We are beholden, not only to God's power, but to his pity, for spiritual supports; and if we have been kept from falling into sin, or shrinking from our duty, we should give him the glory, and encourage our brethren. The psalmist had many troubled thoughts concerning the case he was in, concerning the course he should take, and what was likely to be the end of it. The indulgence of such contrivances and fears, adds to care and distrust, and renders our views more gloomy and confused. Good men sometimes have perplexed and distressed thoughts concerning God. But let them look to the great and precious promises of the gospel. The world's comforts give little delight to the soul, when hurried with melancholy thoughts; but God's comforts bring that peace and pleasure which the smiles of the world cannot give, and which the frowns of the world cannot take away. God is his people's Refuge, to whom they may flee, in whom they are safe, and may be secure. And he will reckon with the wicked. A man cannot be more miserable than his own wickedness will make him, if the Lord visit it upon him.

Worshiping the Lord and our Shepherd (verses 1–7)

Whenever we come into God's presence, we should come with thanksgiving.

There is no shortage of reasons to praise him; the problem is often that our hearts are not ready to do so.

How great is the God to whom the whole earth and everything in it belong!

He directs and disposes of all creation.

The Lord Jesus is the great God whom we are called to praise.

Among his titles are the mighty God and God over all, blessed forever.

He has received authority in heaven and on earth.

He is our God, and we should praise him.

He is our Savior and the source of our true happiness.

The gospel church is his flock.

Christ is the great and good Shepherd who searched for his people when they were lost and brought them safely into his fold.

Editorially restored separate Concise exposition; absent from the pinned MHCC 0.1.1 compiled K body. See source provenance ledger.Hearing Christ's voice today (verses 7–11)

Christ calls his people to listen to his voice.

If we call him Master and Lord, we ought to become willing and obedient servants.

Listen to his teaching, his commandments and the voice of his Spirit speaking through them.

Do not merely hear; pay attention and yield.

We must hear Christ's voice today.

Today's opportunity will not last forever.

We should use it while it remains.

To hear Christ truly is to believe in him.

Hardness of heart lies beneath all distrust of God.

Other people's sins should warn us not to repeat them.

Israel's murmuring in the wilderness was recorded for our instruction.

God is not subject to passions as we are, yet he is truly angry at sin and sinners.

What deserves such a punishment must certainly be evil.

His threats are as certain as his promises.

We must watch the evil tendencies of our hearts, which would draw us away from him.

There is a rest appointed for believers, an eternal refreshment that begins in this life and reaches its fullness in the life to come.

This is the rest God calls his own rest.

Whenever we come into God's presence, we must come with thanksgiving. The Lord is to be praised; we do not want matter, it were well if we did not want a heart. Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA call to all people to praise God.1–9God's government and judgment.10–13
All the earth called to worship (verses 1–9)

When Christ completed his earthly work and was received into heavenly glory, the church began to sing a new song to him and bless his name.

His apostles and evangelists proclaimed his salvation among the nations and his marvelous works among all peoples.

The whole earth is summoned to worship the Lord.

We should worship him in the beauty of holiness, as the God who in Christ reconciles the world to himself.

The glorious truths spoken about Christ are both reasons for praising him and the very substance of our praise.

The coming reign and judgment of Christ (verses 10–13)

We should hope and pray for the time when Christ will reign in righteousness over every nation.

He will rule human hearts through the power of truth and the Spirit of righteousness.

His coming is drawing near.

The King and Judge stands at the door, but the appointed day has not yet arrived.

The Lord welcomes the praise of those who seek the advance of Christ's kingdom.

The sea can roar, but we do not know how trees show their rejoicing.

God searches hearts and knows the mind of the Spirit.

He understands even the halting words and broken language of the weakest.

Christ will come to judge the earth, justly punishing his enemies and fully accomplishing his greatest promises to his people.

What will that day mean for us?

Would we welcome his coming?

If we are not prepared, now is the time to get ready to meet God through forgiveness of our sins and renewal of our hearts in holiness.

Verses 1-9
When Christ finished his work on earth, and was received into his glory in heaven, the church began to sing a new song unto him, and to bless his name. His apostles and evangelists showed forth his salvation among the heathen, his wonders among all people. All the earth is here summoned to worship the Lord. We must worship him in the beauty of holiness, as God in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself. Glorious things are said of him, both as motives to praise and matter of praise.
[Ps.96.10-Ps.96.13]
Verses 10-13
We are to hope and pray for that time, when Christ shall reign in righteousness over all nations. He shall rule in the hearts of men, by the power of truth, and the Spirit of righteousness. His coming draws nigh; this King, this Judge standeth before the door, but he is not yet come. The Lord will accept the praises of all who seek to promote the kingdom of Christ. The sea can but roar, and how the trees of the wood can show that they rejoice we know not; but He that searches the heart knows what is the mind of the Spirit, and understands the words, the broken language of the weakest. Christ will come to judge the earth, to execute just vengeance on his enemies, and to fulfil his largest promises to his people. What then are we? Would that day be welcome to us? If this be not our case, let us now begin to prepare to meet our God, by seeking the pardon of our sins, and the renewal of our souls to holiness.

The irresistible reign of Christ (verses 1–7)

Many have already found happiness in Christ, yet there is still room for others.

All have good reason to rejoice in his reign.

We cannot fully search the depth of his purposes, but righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.

Christ's rule could be a cause of joy for everyone.

Yet for some it will become a cause of terror.

That is their own fault, because they reject him.

Even the most determined and fearless opposition will fail before the Lord.

Jesus Christ will come and bring every form of idolatry to an end.

The Lord's care for those who love him (verses 8–12)

Faithful servants of God rightly rejoice when he is glorified.

Anything that honors him gives pleasure to his people.

God cares for their safety.

But the protection promised goes far beyond preserving their earthly lives.

The Lord will guard his people's souls from sin, apostasy and despair, even under their most severe trials.

He will rescue them from the power of the evil one and bring them safely into his heavenly kingdom.

Those who rejoice in Jesus Christ and his exaltation have sources of joy prepared for them.

People who sow in tears will reap with joy.

Joy is assured to those whose hearts are upright, while a hypocrite's joy lasts only briefly.

Sinners tremble at God's holiness, but his saints rejoice in it.

God hates sin, yet freely loves the repentant sinner who believes in Christ.

He will finally separate the person he loves from the sin he hates, sanctifying his people completely in body, soul and spirit.

Verses 1-7
Though many have been made happy in Christ, still there is room. And all have reason to rejoice in Christ's government. There is a depth in his counsels, which we must not pretend to fathom; but still righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne. Christ's government, though it might be matter of joy to all, will yet be matter of terror to some; but it is their own fault that it is so. The most resolute and daring opposition will be baffled at the presence of the Lord. And the Lord Jesus will ere long come, and put an end to idol worship of every kind.
[Ps.97.8-Ps.97.12]
Verses 8-12
The faithful servants of God may well rejoice and be glad, because he is glorified; and whatever tends to his honour, is his people's pleasure. Care is taken for their safety. But something more is meant than their lives. The Lord will preserve the souls of his saints from sin, from apostacy, and despair, under their greatest trials. He will deliver them out of the hands of the wicked one, and preserve them safe to his heavenly kingdom. And those that rejoice in Christ Jesus, and in his exaltation, have fountains of joy prepared for them. Those that sow in tears, shall reap in joy. Gladness is sure to the upright in heart; the joy of the hypocrite is but for a moment. Sinners tremble, but saints rejoice at God's holiness. As he hates sin, yet freely loves the person of the repentant sinner who believes in Christ, he will make a final separation between the person he loves and the sin he hates, and sanctify his people wholly, body, soul, and spirit.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe glory of the Redeemer.1–3The joy of the Redeemer.4–9
Singing a new song for redemption (verses 1–3)

The song of redeeming love is new because it celebrates a mystery hidden from earlier ages and generations.

Those converted to Christ sing in a new way, very different from their former songs.

If God puts a new heart within us, he also gives us a new song.

We should sing it to his praise because of the marvelous works he has accomplished.

The Redeemer overcame every obstacle in the way of our salvation.

Neither the services nor the sufferings appointed for him discouraged him.

Praise the Lord for revealing his salvation and righteousness to the world, fulfilling the Old Testament prophecies and promises.

To accomplish this purpose, God sent his Son Jesus not only as a light to the nations, but also as the glory of Israel.

We should examine whether his holy arm has won the victory within our hearts, overcoming Satan, unbelief and sin.

If he has, we will exchange shallow songs of vanity for songs of gladness and thanksgiving.

Our lives will proclaim the Redeemer's praise.

The whole creation invited to rejoice (verses 4–9)

Everyone has reason to rejoice in the establishment of Christ's kingdom, because all may benefit from it.

The psalm seems to use figurative language to describe different orders of rational creatures throughout the universe rejoicing under the great Messiah's reign.

Christ's kingdom will bring blessing to the whole creation.

We await his second coming, when his glorious reign will be fully displayed.

Then heaven and earth will rejoice, and the joy of the redeemed will be complete.

But sin and its devastating consequences will not be entirely removed until the Lord comes to judge the world in righteousness.

Because we await these things, we should strive to be found by him at peace, spotless and blameless.
classic_reading:
[Ps.98.1-Ps.98.3]
Chapter 98
Chapter Outline
The glory of the Redeemer. | (1-3) |
The joy of the Redeemer. | (4-9) |
Verses 1-3
A song of praise for redeeming love is a new song, a mystery hidden from ages and generations. Converts sing a new song, very different from what they had sung. If the grace of God put a new heart into our breasts, it will put a new song into our mouths. Let this new song be sung to the praise of God, in consideration of the wonders he has wrought. The Redeemer has overcome all difficulties in the way of our redemption, and was not discouraged by the services or sufferings appointed him. Let us praise him for the discoveries made to the world of the work of redemption; his salvation and his righteousness fulfilling the prophecies and promises of the Old Testament. In pursuance of this design, God raised up his Son Jesus to be not only a Light to lighten the Gentiles, but the glory of his people Israel. Surely it behoves us to inquire whether his holy arm hath gotten the victory in our hearts, over the power of Satan, unbelief, and sin? If this be our happy case, we shall exchange all light songs of vanity for songs of joy and thanksgiving; our lives will celebrate the Redeemer's praise.
[Ps.98.4-Ps.98.9]
Verses 4-9
Let all the children of men rejoice in the setting up the kingdom of Christ, for all may benefit by it. The different orders of rational creatures in the universe, seem to be described in figurative language in the reign of the great Messiah. The kingdom of Christ will be a blessing to the whole creation. We expect his second coming to begin his glorious reign. Then shall heaven and earth rejoice, and the joy of the redeemed shall be full. But sin and its dreadful effects will not be utterly done away, till the Lord come to judge the world in righteousness. Seeing then that we look for such things, let us give diligence that we may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe happy government God's people are under.1–5Its happy administration.6–9
God's holy government (verses 1–5)

God governs the world through his providence and governs the church through his grace.

He governs both through his Son.

Earth's inhabitants have reason to tremble before him.

Yet the Redeemer still waits to show mercy.

Everyone who hears his warning should seek his grace.

The more we humble ourselves before the Lord, the more truly we exalt him.

We should worship with reverence because he is holy.

God's servants call upon him (verses 6–9)

Israel's happiness is illustrated by the leaders who served the people best.

They made God's word and law their standard in everything, knowing that without obedience they could not expect their prayers to be heard.

They repeatedly prevailed in prayer.

The Lord performed miracles in answer to their requests.

They interceded for the people and received gracious answers bringing peace.

But our Prophet and High Priest is of infinitely greater dignity than Moses, Aaron or Samuel.

He has received and declared the Father's will to us.

Therefore, do not exalt God with your lips alone.

Give him the throne in your heart.

As we worship before his mercy seat, remember always that he is holy.
classic_reading:
[Ps.99.1-Ps.99.5]
Chapter 99
Chapter Outline
The happy government God's people are under. | (1-5) |
Its happy administration. | (6-9) |
Verses 1-5
God governs the world by his providence, governs the church by his grace, and both by his Son. The inhabitants of the earth have cause to tremble, but the Redeemer still waits to be gracious. Let all who hear, take warning, and seek his mercy. The more we humble ourselves before God, the more we exalt him; and let us be thus reverent, for he is holy.
[Ps.99.6-Ps.99.9]
Verses 6-9
The happiness of Israel is made out by referring to the most useful governors of that people. They in every thing made God's word and law their rule, knowing that they could not else expect that their prayers should be answered. They all wonderfully prevailed with God in prayer; miracles were wrought at their request. They pleaded for the people, and obtained answers of peace. Our Prophet and High Priest, of infinitely greater dignity than Moses, Aaron, or Samuel, has received and declared to us the will of the Father. Let us not only exalt the Lord with our lips, but give him the throne in our heart; and while we worship him upon his mercy-seat, let us never forget that he is holy.

modern_osis:
Original heading

An exhortation to praise God, and rejoice in him.

The whole earth called to joyful worship

This psalm of praise can be read as a prophecy and also offered as a prayer for the day when people everywhere will know that the Lord is God.

They will become his worshipers and the sheep of his pasture.

We have strong encouragement to worship him cheerfully.

We had wandered like sheep.

If God has brought us back into his fold, we have abundant reason to bless his name.

The reasons and themes of our praise are of the highest importance.

Know God for who he is, and understand who he is to you.

Consider these truths and apply them to your life.

Doing so will make your worship more faithful and regular, more heartfelt and earnest.

The covenant of grace is revealed throughout the Scriptures of both Old and New Testaments.

Its rich promises strengthen the faith of even the weakest believer.

They provide a firm foundation for our praise and joy.

When we look at ourselves, our spirits may be heavy and full of sorrow.

But when we look toward God's goodness, mercy and the promises of his word, we find many reasons to give thanks and receive comfort.

An exhortation to praise God, and rejoice in him.
--This song of praise should be considered as a prophecy, and even used as a prayer, for the coming of that time when all people shall know that the Lord he is God, and shall become his worshippers, and the sheep of his pasture. Great encouragement is given us, in worshipping God, to do it cheerfully. If, when we strayed like wandering sheep, he has brought us again to his fold, we have indeed abundant cause to bless his name. The matter of praise, and the motives to it, are very important. Know ye what God is in himself, and what he is to you. Know it; consider and apply it, then you will be more close and constant, more inward and serious, in his worship. The covenant of grace set down in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament, with so many rich promises, to strengthen the faith of every weak believer, makes the matter of God's praise and of his people's joys so sure, that how sad soever our spirits may be when we look to ourselves, yet we shall have reason to praise the Lord when we look to his goodness and mercy, and to what he has said in his word for our comfort.
